title: Preparation, Properties and Uses of Benzene
topicTitle: Preparation of benzene from decarboxylation of sodium benzoate, phenol, and ethyne only; physical properties of benzene; chemical properties of benzene; combustion of benzene (free combustion only) and uses
notes: **Decarboxylation of sodium benzoate:** heating sodium benzoate with soda lime (NaOH + CaO) removes the carboxyl group as $CO_2$, yielding benzene: $C_6H_5COONa + NaOH \xrightarrow{CaO,\; \Delta} C_6H_6 + Na_2CO_3$. This is a classic laboratory method. CaO serves as a support to prevent caking and absorbs moisture. The reaction proceeds via a carbanion intermediate after base-induced decarboxylation.

**Reduction of phenol to benzene:** phenol is reduced by passing its vapours over zinc dust at red heat: $C_6H_5OH + Zn \xrightarrow{\Delta} C_6H_6 + ZnO$. The Zn removes the oxygen as ZnO, effectively reducing the C–O bond. This method is valuable because it demonstrates that the aromatic ring survives reduction conditions that would saturate alkenes.

**Trimerization of ethyne (acetylene):** passing ethyne through a red-hot iron tube at 873 K causes cyclic trimerization: $3C_2H_2 \xrightarrow{red\; hot\; Fe,\; 873\; K} C_6H_6$. This is an example of alkyne cyclotrimerization, where three $\pi$ bonds are rearranged to form the aromatic ring. The reaction is catalyzed by transition metals and proceeds via a metallacycle intermediate.

**Physical state and appearance:** benzene is a colourless, transparent liquid at room temperature with a distinctive sweet, aromatic odour (characteristic of many aromatic compounds). It is highly volatile (bp 80.1°C) and flammable. The name 'aromatic' originally referred to this pleasant smell, though not all aromatic compounds smell good.

**Density and solubility:** benzene has a density of 0.8765 g/cm³ at 20°C, making it less dense than water (0.9998 g/cm³). It is immiscible with water but miscible with most organic solvents (ethanol, ether, acetone, carbon tetrachloride). This makes benzene an excellent non-polar solvent.

**Melting point anomaly:** benzene has an unusually high melting point (5.5°C) for a hydrocarbon of its molecular weight, due to its high symmetry allowing efficient packing in the crystal lattice. This is why benzene solidifies on a cool day — pure benzene freezes just below typical room temperature.

**Electrophilic aromatic substitution — Nitration:** benzene reacts with a mixture of concentrated $HNO_3$ and concentrated $H_2SO_4$ at 50–60°C to form nitrobenzene: $C_6H_6 + HNO_3 \xrightarrow{H_2SO_4} C_6H_5NO_2 + H_2O$. The electrophile is the nitronium ion $NO_2^+$, generated by protonation of nitric acid followed by loss of water: $HNO_3 + 2H_2SO_4 \rightarrow NO_2^+ + H_3O^+ + 2HSO_4^-$.

**Electrophilic aromatic substitution — Halogenation:** benzene reacts with $Cl_2$ or $Br_2$ in the presence of a Lewis acid catalyst ($FeCl_3$, $FeBr_3$, or $AlCl_3$) to give chlorobenzene or bromobenzene: $C_6H_6 + Cl_2 \xrightarrow{FeCl_3} C_6H_5Cl + HCl$. The Lewis acid polarizes the halogen molecule, generating a stronger electrophile ($Cl^+$ or $Br^+$ character). Without the catalyst, no reaction occurs at room temperature.

**Electrophilic aromatic substitution — Sulphonation:** benzene reacts with concentrated $H_2SO_4$ (or oleum, $H_2SO_4 + SO_3$) upon heating to form benzenesulphonic acid: $C_6H_6 + H_2SO_4 \rightleftharpoons C_6H_5SO_3H + H_2O$. The electrophile is sulphur trioxide ($SO_3$) or protonated $SO_3H^+$. This reaction is reversible — benzenesulphonic acid is converted back to benzene by heating with dilute acid (steam desulphonation).

**Friedel-Crafts reactions:** (i) **Alkylation:** benzene reacts with an alkyl halide in the presence of $AlCl_3$ to give an alkylbenzene: $C_6H_6 + CH_3Cl \xrightarrow{AlCl_3} C_6H_5CH_3 + HCl$. (ii) **Acylation:** benzene reacts with an acyl chloride to give an aryl ketone: $C_6H_6 + CH_3COCl \xrightarrow{AlCl_3} C_6H_5COCH_3 + HCl$. These reactions introduce carbon chains onto the ring and are among the most important C–C bond-forming reactions in organic synthesis.

**Addition reactions (under forcing conditions):** although benzene resists addition, it can undergo addition under extreme conditions. **Catalytic hydrogenation:** $C_6H_6 + 3H_2 \xrightarrow{Ni,\; 180°C,\; high\; pressure} C_6H_{12}$ (cyclohexane). **Photochlorination:** $C_6H_6 + 3Cl_2 \xrightarrow{UV\; light} C_6H_6Cl_6$ (1,2,3,4,5,6-hexachlorocyclohexane, known as benzene hexachloride or BHC/Gammaxene, formerly used as an insecticide). These reactions destroy aromaticity and require significant energy input.

**Combustion of benzene (free combustion):** benzene burns with a sooty yellow flame due to its high carbon content (92.3% by mass). In excess air: $2C_6H_6 + 15O_2 \rightarrow 12CO_2 + 6H_2O + heat$ ($\Delta H_c = -3268$ kJ/mol). The soot forms because the dense pi electron cloud makes complete oxidation difficult in limited air — fine carbon particles are released as smoke. This sooty flame is a test for aromaticity.

**Oxidation of benzene:** benzene is remarkably resistant to oxidation. It does not decolorize acidic $KMnO_4$ or bromine water (unlike alkenes). However, at high temperature with a vanadium catalyst, it can be oxidized to maleic anhydride: $C_6H_6 + 4.5O_2 \xrightarrow{V_2O_5,\; \Delta} C_4H_2O_3 + 2CO_2 + 2H_2O$. This is an important industrial process for producing maleic anhydride.

**Uses of benzene:** (1) Industrial feedstock — the single largest use is as a precursor to ethylbenzene (for styrene/polystyrene), cyclohexane (for nylon), and cumene (for phenol/acetone). (2) Solvent — formerly used as an industrial solvent for fats, oils, waxes, resins, and in dry cleaning; its use has declined due to carcinogenicity. (3) Gasoline additive — benzene was added to petrol to increase octane rating, but modern fuels are restricted to <1% benzene by volume due to health concerns. (4) Chemical synthesis — precursor to detergents, dyes, drugs (e.g., aspirin from salicylic acid derived from phenol), and pesticides.

**Safety and toxicity:** benzene is a confirmed human carcinogen (Group 1, IARC). Chronic exposure causes aplastic anemia, leukemia (especially acute myeloid leukemia), and bone marrow suppression. It is metabolized in the liver to toxic intermediates including benzene oxide and benzoquinone, which damage DNA. Occupational exposure limits are typically 0.5–1 ppm (8-hour time-weighted average). Many laboratory applications have been replaced by toluene, which has similar solvent properties but significantly lower toxicity.

**Physical constants summary:** molecular formula $C_6H_6$, molecular mass = 78.11 g/mol, melting point = 5.5°C, boiling point = 80.1°C, density = 0.8765 g/cm³ (20°C), refractive index $n_D^{20} = 1.5011$, enthalpy of combustion = -3268 kJ/mol, enthalpy of formation = +49.0 kJ/mol (positive! indicating instability relative to elements, yet stabilized by resonance). Benzene is miscible with ethanol, ether, acetone, and $CCl_4$.
confusion: Misconception: Benzene decolorizes bromine water like alkenes do. — Correct explanation: Benzene does NOT decolorize bromine water at room temperature because it does not undergo addition reactions under mild conditions. The aromatic pi system is too stable. Bromine water testing is a standard qualitative test to distinguish benzene (no reaction) from alkenes (rapid decolorization). Benzene only reacts with bromine in the presence of a Lewis acid catalyst (FeBr₃) via substitution, not addition.

Misconception: The combustion of benzene produces only CO₂ and H₂O with a clean blue flame. — Correct explanation: Benzene burns with a characteristic sooty yellow flame due to its high carbon-to-hydrogen ratio (C:H = 1:1 by atoms, 92.3% C by mass). Incomplete combustion produces fine carbon particles (soot) that glow yellow. This sooty flame is a hallmark of aromatic compounds and distinguishes them from aliphatic hydrocarbons, which burn with cleaner flames.

Misconception: Benzene is used as a common laboratory solvent today. — Correct explanation: While benzene was widely used as a solvent historically, its use has been largely abandoned in laboratories and industry because it is a potent carcinogen. Toluene (methylbenzene) is now the standard replacement — it has similar solvent properties and a boiling point of 110.6°C, but is significantly less toxic. Always check the Safety Data Sheet (SDS) before using any aromatic solvent.

Misconception: Friedel-Crafts alkylation always gives high yields of the desired product. — Correct explanation: Friedel-Crafts alkylation has several limitations: (1) Carbocation rearrangement can occur, giving unexpected products (e.g., n-propyl chloride gives isopropylbenzene, not n-propylbenzene). (2) Polyalkylation is common because the product is more reactive than the starting material. (3) The reaction fails with strong electron-withdrawing groups already on the ring (e.g., nitrobenzene). Friedel-Crafts acylation avoids rearrangement and polyacylation, making it often preferable.
practice: Problem: Write balanced equations for the preparation of benzene from (a) sodium benzoate, (b) phenol, and (c) ethyne. Identify the type of reaction in each case. — Solution: (a) $C_6H_5COONa + NaOH \xrightarrow{CaO,\; \Delta} C_6H_6 + Na_2CO_3$ — decarboxylation (removal of CO₂ as carbonate). (b) $C_6H_5OH + Zn \xrightarrow{\Delta} C_6H_6 + ZnO$ — reduction (Zn removes oxygen as ZnO). (c) $3C_2H_2 \xrightarrow{red\; hot\; Fe,\; 873\; K} C_6H_6$ — cyclic trimerization / cyclotrimerization of alkynes.

Problem: Benzene undergoes nitration at 50–60°C but requires 100°C for sulphonation. Explain this difference in reactivity and predict the product of each reaction. — Solution: The electrophile in nitration ($NO_2^+$) is a very strong electrophile, generated in situ by the powerful dehydrating action of $H_2SO_4$ on $HNO_3$. It attacks benzene readily at moderate temperatures (50–60°C). The electrophile in sulphonation ($SO_3$ or $HSO_3^+$) is less reactive than $NO_2^+$, so higher temperatures (~100°C) or fuming sulphuric acid (oleum) are needed. Products: nitration gives nitrobenzene ($C_6H_5NO_2$); sulphonation gives benzenesulphonic acid ($C_6H_5SO_3H$).

Problem: A sample of benzene (7.8 g) is completely combusted in excess oxygen. Calculate the volume of CO₂ produced at STP and the mass of water formed. (Atomic masses: C = 12, H = 1) — Solution: Moles of benzene $= 7.8 / 78 = 0.1$ mol. From the equation $2C_6H_6 + 15O_2 \rightarrow 12CO_2 + 6H_2O$: 0.1 mol benzene produces $0.1 \times 6 = 0.6$ mol $CO_2$ and $0.1 \times 3 = 0.3$ mol $H_2O$. Volume of $CO_2$ at STP $= 0.6 \times 22.4 = 13.44$ L. Mass of $H_2O = 0.3 \times 18 = 5.4$ g.

Problem: Arrange the following in order of decreasing reactivity toward electrophilic substitution: benzene, nitrobenzene, toluene, chlorobenzene. Explain your reasoning. — Solution: Toluene > benzene > chlorobenzene > nitrobenzene. CH₃ is an electron-donating group (inductive + hyperconjugation), activating the ring and directing ortho/para. Cl is electron-withdrawing by induction but electron-donating by resonance; the inductive effect dominates, making it weakly deactivating but ortho/para-directing. NO₂ is strongly electron-withdrawing by both induction and resonance, making nitrobenzene the least reactive (about 10⁶ times less reactive than benzene) and meta-directing.

Problem: Explain why benzene hexachloride (BHC, C₆H₆Cl₆) is prepared by reacting benzene with Cl₂ under UV light, whereas chlorobenzene (C₆H₅Cl) is prepared using Cl₂ with FeCl₃. What type of mechanism operates in each case? — Solution: With FeCl₃ catalyst, Cl₂ is polarized to generate the electrophile Cl⁺, which attacks the aromatic ring via electrophilic substitution, giving chlorobenzene and HCl. Under UV light, Cl₂ undergoes homolytic cleavage to form chlorine radicals (Cl•). These radicals add across the double bonds of benzene in a free-radical addition mechanism, saturating the ring to give 1,2,3,4,5,6-hexachlorocyclohexane (BHC). The key difference is: ionic/electrophilic conditions give substitution (preserving aromaticity), while radical/UV conditions give addition (destroying aromaticity).
universalFacts: Benzene is the parent compound of the entire class of aromatic hydrocarbons. Over 90% of produced benzene is converted into three key derivatives: ethylbenzene (for polystyrene), cumene (for phenol and acetone), and cyclohexane (for nylon), making it indispensable to the plastics and fibers industry.

The positive enthalpy of formation of benzene (+49 kJ/mol) is remarkable — it means benzene is thermodynamically unstable with respect to its elements (graphite and H₂ gas). However, its kinetic stability (high activation energy for breaking aromaticity) means it persists indefinitely under normal conditions.

The sooty flame test is a quick qualitative method to identify aromatic compounds. The high carbon content (92.3% for benzene) leads to incomplete combustion and the release of incandescent carbon particles. Aliphatic hydrocarbons with lower C:H ratios burn with cleaner flames.

The industrial importance of benzene's chemistry is so vast that the benzene production capacity of a nation is often used as an indicator of its petrochemical industrial strength. Global benzene production exceeded 85 million tonnes annually in the 2020s.

The replacement of benzene with toluene as a laboratory and industrial solvent represents one of the most important safety improvements in 20th-century chemistry. Toluene retains benzene's excellent solvent properties (non-polar, miscible with organics, bp 110.6°C) while being significantly less toxic and non-carcinogenic.
